html:
The Samanid Mausoleum is a small brick tomb in Bukhara, in today's Uzbekistan, built in the late 9th or early 10th century. It is one of the oldest and most admired buildings of early Islamic Central Asia.

It was the family tomb of the Samanids, the Persian dynasty that ruled from Bukhara, and is linked to Ismail Samani, the ruler who made it their capital. Under the Samanids, Bukhara was a centre of Persian poetry and learning.

The building is a near perfect cube topped by a dome, about ten metres on each side. Its fame comes from the brick. Baked bricks are laid in patterns that look like woven baskets, so the walls seem to shift as the sun moves across them. The form of a domed cube recalls the fire temples of the old Sasanian religion.

It survived the Mongol conquest of 1220, perhaps because it lay half buried in earth and sand. Soviet archaeologists cleared it in the 1930s. Its brick craft looks forward to later Bukhara buildings such as the Kalyan Minaret.
